Monthly, biweekly or accelerated: separate payment timing from paying more

Four charts compare remaining debt, the first year’s payment budget and interest to payoff, using explicit Canadian mortgage rate and payment conventions.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare payment frequency and the annual cash commitment

Interactive planning lab

Hypothetical rate stays unchanged for the entire amortization; this is not a mortgage quote or renewal forecast. Nominal rate compounds semi-annually and is converted to 12 or 26 equal periods per model year. Monthly payment amortizes the starting principal over the selected years; regular biweekly is monthly × 12 ÷ 26, accelerated biweekly is monthly ÷ 2. Interest accrues on opening debt and payments occur at period-end. Final payment is capped. No fees, tax, prepayment restrictions, daily calendar, holiday shift or cents rounding.

The central idea

Accelerated biweekly payments change the annual cash commitment as well as the payment dates. Compare both before attributing the interest difference to frequency alone.

01

Start with three clearly defined payment rules

A mortgage payment can become smaller each time it leaves the account while the total paid during a year becomes larger. The labels matter because “biweekly” and “accelerated biweekly” describe different cash commitments.

The FCAC’s mortgage-selection guide defines regular biweekly as the monthly payment multiplied by twelve and divided by twenty-six. Accelerated biweekly uses half the monthly payment on each of twenty-six payment occasions. That second rule produces thirteen monthly-payment equivalents in a full scheduled year.

The charts apply those payment definitions to one hypothetical opening mortgage. They keep the selected rate unchanged through payoff to isolate the mechanics. An actual mortgage has a term, renewal conditions and contractual payment provisions that can change the path. No future renewal rate is inferred from the example.

02

Convert the rate before calculating each period’s interest

The example starts with CAD 400,000, a twenty-five-year amortization and a hypothetical 5% nominal annual rate compounded semi-annually. The equivalent monthly rate is (1 + 0.05 ÷ 2)2/12 − 1, rather than 5% divided by twelve.

At a payment frequency f, the equivalent rate per payment period is (1 + nominal annual rate ÷ 2)2/f − 1. Compounding that rate for f equal model periods recovers the same effective annual rate. For the monthly payment, the model uses three hundred scheduled periods and the ordinary amortizing-payment equation.

A model year contains exactly twelve monthly periods or twenty-six biweekly periods. This is an equal-period comparison, rather than a calendar with exact fourteen-day intervals and occasional twenty-seventh payment dates. Payment amounts are retained at full precision; a lender’s cents rounding and dated interest calculations can produce different final figures.

03

Reconcile each payment with a full year’s budget

The calculated monthly payment is about CAD 2,326.42, or CAD 27,917.04 over twelve scheduled payments. Regular biweekly is about CAD 1,073.73 on each occasion, giving the same CAD 27,917.04 annual scheduled total before final-payment adjustments.

Accelerated biweekly is about CAD 1,163.21 each time. Twenty-six such payments schedule about CAD 30,243.46 a year. The difference is about CAD 2,326.42, equal to one extra monthly-payment equivalent.

The first-year stacked bars divide actual cash paid between principal and interest. A principal payment reduces the liability; interest is the cost of borrowing. The accelerated path has more principal reduction in part because it receives more cash. Its lower individual payment than the monthly amount should not be read as a smaller annual commitment.

04

Follow each balance to its own payoff date

Under the unchanged default rate, the monthly path finishes at twenty-five model years. Regular biweekly finishes after six hundred and forty-nine equal periods, or about 24.96 model years. It pays about CAD 296,401.90 of interest, compared with about CAD 297,925.98 for monthly payments.

The accelerated path finishes after five hundred and fifty-nine periods, or 21.50 model years. Its modeled interest is about CAD 249,577.30. The difference from monthly payments is about CAD 48,348.69 under these assumptions.

That larger difference combines timing with higher annual payments; it is not the isolated value of moving the same cash to different dates. Each curve stops at its own payoff, and the last payment is reduced to the balance plus accrued period interest. No additional full payment is collected after the mortgage reaches zero.

05

Use the matrix to compare rates without hiding payment changes

The matrix replaces the nominal annual rate and calculates all three payment methods again. Principal and original amortization remain fixed, but the base monthly payment is recalculated for each rate row. Cells show interest to the relevant payoff date.

Read across a row to compare methods at one rate. Reading down a column changes both interest and the payment required by the same original amortization. It is not a test that holds the current payment fixed after a rate increase.

At a zero rate, interest is zero for every method. Accelerated repayment can still finish sooner because it schedules more principal during a model year. This boundary helps separate a payment-speed result from an interest-cost result.

06

Choose a schedule that fits cash arriving in the household

Compare the proposed dates with actual net-pay receipts and existing bill dates. A biweekly salary does not guarantee that a mortgage debit falls after it. Keep enough accessible cash for the period before the first receipt, rather than relying only on the annual surplus.

Confirm whether the lender permits the payment-frequency change, how it calculates the new amount and whether any payment increase counts against a contractual privilege. The model does not assess penalties, product eligibility or the effect of an upcoming renewal.

A useful planning record contains the payment amount, scheduled yearly total, principal path and the cash buffer needed between dates. Those four measures show the practical trade-off: more cash directed to the mortgage can reduce debt sooner, but that cash also needs to fit the wider household plan.
